Topics.Title: Foundations of Local Search
Topics.Summary: Introduces local search as optimization over complete states, where only the final configuration matters and the path to it is irrelevant. Contrasts this approach with systematic path-finding search in terms of memory use, completeness, and suitability for very large or infinite state spaces.

Elements.Title: What Local Search Is
Elements.BodyText: Local search is an optimization-style approach that operates on complete candidate states rather than partial paths. It moves from one full configuration to a neighbouring one, trying to improve a quality measure.
Elements.Notes: Example: in the 8-queens problem, a state is a full board with all eight queens placed, and a move shifts one queen within its column.

Items.Text: Each node in local search is a complete, valid configuration of the problem.
The algorithm keeps a current state and repeatedly replaces it with a neighbour.
Neighbours are generated by small, local modifications to the current state.
Progress is measured by an objective or cost function rather than by distance from a start node.

Elements.Title: When the Path Does Not Matter
Elements.BodyText: Local search is appropriate when only the final configuration is a solution, not the sequence of moves that produced it. This is the defining distinction from classical path-finding search.
Elements.Notes: Contrast: route finding needs the path itself; n-queens, scheduling and VLSI layout only need the final arrangement.

Items.Text: Problems such as n-queens, job scheduling, timetabling and circuit layout care only about the end state.
In route planning or puzzle solving, the path is the answer and local search is unsuitable.
Because the path is irrelevant, no search tree or parent pointers need to be stored.
Goal tests are often replaced by an objective function to maximise or a cost to minimise.

Elements.Title: The State-Space Landscape
Elements.BodyText: Local search is often visualised as navigating a landscape where location represents a state and elevation represents the objective function value. The algorithm tries to find the highest peak or lowest valley.
Elements.Notes: The same algorithm can be described as hill climbing (maximisation) or gradient descent (minimisation) depending on the sign of the objective.

Items.Text: Elevation corresponds to the objective value for maximisation or cost for minimisation.
A global maximum is the best state overall in the entire landscape.
Local maxima, plateaus and ridges are landscape features that can trap a search.
The algorithm can only perceive the landscape immediately around its current state.

Elements.Title: Memory and Efficiency Advantages
Elements.BodyText: Because local search retains only the current state and its immediate neighbours, memory use is typically constant. This makes it practical where systematic search would exhaust available resources.

Items.Text: No frontier or explored set needs to be maintained, unlike BFS or A*.
Memory requirements remain small and usually independent of problem size.
Local search can run on state spaces too large to enumerate, including continuous and infinite ones.
It can often find reasonable solutions quickly, even when optimal search is intractable.

Elements.Title: Completeness and Optimality Trade-offs
Elements.BodyText: The efficiency of local search comes at a cost: it offers no guarantee of finding a solution or of finding the best one. Understanding these limitations is essential when choosing the method.
Elements.Notes: Randomised restarts and stochastic moves are common ways to mitigate incompleteness in practice.

Items.Text: Local search is generally incomplete, as it may become stuck before reaching a goal.
It is not optimal, since it may settle on a local rather than global optimum.
Systematic search offers completeness guarantees but can require exponential memory.
In practice, anytime behaviour is valuable: a usable solution is available whenever the search is stopped.

Topics.Title: State Spaces, Objective Functions, and Landscapes
Topics.Summary: Explains how problems are framed for local search using complete-state formulations, neighbor/move operators, and objective or heuristic cost functions. Uses the state-space landscape metaphor of peaks, valleys, ridges, shoulders, and plateaus to visualize search behavior.

Elements.Title: Complete-State Formulation
Elements.BodyText: Local search abandons the idea of building a solution step by step from an initial state. Instead, every state in the search space is already a complete candidate solution that can be evaluated and improved.
Elements.Notes: Example: in the 8-queens problem, a complete state places all eight queens on the board (often one per column) rather than adding queens one at a time.

Items.Text: Each state is a full assignment of all variables or decisions in the problem.
The search moves from one complete solution to another, never through partial solutions.
The path taken to reach a state is irrelevant — only the final state matters.
Memory use is typically constant, since only the current state (and perhaps a best-so-far) is retained.
This makes local search viable for very large or even infinite state spaces where systematic search is infeasible.

Elements.Title: Neighbors and Move Operators
Elements.BodyText: A move operator defines which states are reachable in one step from the current state, generating its neighborhood. The choice of operator determines the shape and connectivity of the search space.
Elements.Notes: For 8-queens, a common operator moves a single queen within its column, yielding 8 × 7 = 56 neighbors.

Items.Text: The neighborhood is the set of all states reachable by a single application of the move operator.
Small neighborhoods are cheap to evaluate but may trap the search; large neighborhoods cost more per step but explore better.
Typical operators include swapping two elements, flipping a variable's value, or shifting one component.
A well-designed operator keeps neighbors structurally similar so that cost changes can be computed incrementally.
The operator must connect the space well enough that an optimal solution is reachable from any starting point.

Elements.Title: Objective and Heuristic Cost Functions
Elements.BodyText: Local search needs a numeric evaluation of state quality to decide which neighbor to move to. This is expressed either as an objective function to maximize or a cost/heuristic function to minimize.
Elements.Notes: For 8-queens, h(state) = the number of pairs of queens attacking each other; a solution has h = 0.

Items.Text: Maximization and minimization are interchangeable: minimizing h is the same as maximizing −h.
The function must be defined for every complete state, not just goal states.
A good evaluation function gives gradient information, steadily guiding the search toward better regions.
Flat or coarse-grained functions give the search no direction and degrade performance.
Evaluation is called very often, so it should be cheap or incrementally updatable.

Elements.Title: The State-Space Landscape Metaphor
Elements.BodyText: Visualizing the search space as a landscape makes local search behavior intuitive. The horizontal dimensions represent states, and elevation represents the value of the objective function.
Elements.Notes: Under a cost function the metaphor inverts: the search descends into valleys instead of climbing to peaks.

Items.Text: Hill climbing seeks the highest peak — the global maximum — by always moving uphill.
A complete local search algorithm always finds a goal if one exists; an optimal one always finds the global maximum.
Real landscapes are high-dimensional, so the 2D or 3D picture is only an aid to intuition.
The ruggedness of the landscape — how many peaks and how far apart they are — predicts how hard the problem is for local search.

Elements.Title: Landscape Features: Peaks, Valleys, Ridges, Shoulders, and Plateaus
Elements.BodyText: Specific landscape shapes explain why local search succeeds or fails. Recognizing these features motivates the variants and escape strategies used in practice.
Elements.Notes: Distinguishing a shoulder from a flat local maximum matters: sideways moves help on a shoulder but loop forever on a true flat maximum.

Items.Text: A local maximum is a peak higher than all its neighbors but lower than the global maximum, where simple hill climbing halts.
A plateau is a flat region where all neighbors have equal value, leaving the search with no gradient to follow.
A shoulder is a plateau from which uphill progress is still possible if the search moves sideways long enough.
A ridge is a sequence of local maxima with steep sides that single-step operators must climb in an awkward zigzag.
Valleys and basins are the minimization-view equivalents of peaks and plateaus.

Elements.Title: Framing a Problem for Local Search
Elements.BodyText: Turning a real problem into a local search instance requires four design decisions. Each choice directly affects how smooth and navigable the resulting landscape is.
Elements.Notes: Typical applications include the n-queens problem, VLSI layout, job-shop scheduling, vehicle routing, and telecommunications network design.

Items.Text: Define the state representation so that every state is a complete, legal candidate.
Choose a move operator that produces a tractable and well-connected neighborhood.
Design an evaluation function that smoothly discriminates between good and bad states.
Decide a starting policy: random initialization, a greedy construction, or multiple restarts.
Set a termination condition such as finding a zero-cost state, exhausting iterations, or detecting no improvement.

Topics.Title: Hill Climbing and Its Variants
Topics.Summary: Describes the basic greedy hill-climbing algorithm and its loop of moving to the best neighboring state. Covers steepest-ascent, first-choice, stochastic, and random-restart hill climbing, comparing their trade-offs in efficiency and solution quality.

Elements.Title: Local Search and Complete-State Formulation
Elements.BodyText: Hill climbing belongs to the family of local search algorithms, which operate on a single complete candidate solution rather than building a path from an initial state. This makes them suited to optimization problems where the goal state itself matters, not how you reached it.
Elements.Notes: Example: in the 8-queens problem, every state has all eight queens on the board; moves shift a queen within its column rather than adding queens one at a time.

Items.Text: A state is a complete configuration that can be evaluated by an objective (or cost) function.
Neighbours are states reachable by a single small modification of the current state.
Memory use is minimal because only the current state (and sometimes its best neighbour) is stored.
Local search is applicable to very large or infinite state spaces where systematic search is infeasible.
The search landscape can be pictured as a surface of states with elevation equal to the objective value.

Elements.Title: The Basic Hill-Climbing Loop
Elements.BodyText: Hill climbing is a greedy loop that repeatedly moves to a neighbouring state with a better objective value. It terminates when no neighbour is an improvement over the current state.
Elements.Notes: Sometimes described as 'climbing Everest in thick fog with amnesia' — the algorithm only sees the immediate neighbourhood and remembers nothing of where it has been.

Items.Text: Start from a randomly generated or heuristically chosen complete state.
Generate the neighbours of the current state and evaluate each with the objective function.
If the best neighbour improves on the current state, move there; otherwise return the current state as the answer.
The algorithm keeps no search tree, no frontier, and no record of visited states.
Because it never moves downhill, it is fast but offers no guarantee of finding the global optimum.

Elements.Title: Steepest-Ascent Hill Climbing
Elements.BodyText: Steepest-ascent is the standard form of hill climbing, in which all neighbours are examined and the single best one is selected. It makes the locally optimal choice at every step.
Elements.Notes: In 8-queens, steepest ascent evaluates all 56 possible single-queen moves before committing to one.

Items.Text: Every successor must be generated and scored before a move is made.
The move chosen is the one with the greatest improvement in objective value.
This yields rapid progress per step but can be expensive when the branching factor is large.
It is most vulnerable to getting stuck, since it always follows the same deterministic path from a given start.

Elements.Title: First-Choice Hill Climbing
Elements.BodyText: First-choice hill climbing generates successors at random and accepts the first one that is better than the current state. It avoids the cost of evaluating the entire neighbourhood.

Items.Text: Successors are produced one at a time in random order until an improvement is found.
This is a practical strategy when a state has thousands of neighbours.
Each step is cheaper, though the move taken may be a smaller improvement than the steepest one.
Different runs from the same start can follow different trajectories because of the random ordering.

Elements.Title: Stochastic Hill Climbing
Elements.BodyText: Stochastic hill climbing chooses at random among the uphill moves available, often weighting the choice by how steep each move is. It trades some greediness for broader exploration.
Elements.Notes: Steeper moves can be given a higher probability of selection, so the search still favours strong improvements without always committing to the single best one.

Items.Text: Only improving (uphill) moves are candidates, but the best is not automatically taken.
Selection probability can be proportional to the size of the improvement.
Convergence is usually slower than steepest ascent in number of iterations.
The added randomness often produces better final solutions on rugged landscapes.

Elements.Title: Random-Restart Hill Climbing
Elements.BodyText: Random-restart hill climbing runs the basic algorithm repeatedly from randomly generated starting states and keeps the best result found. It directly attacks the problem of getting trapped in a poor local optimum.
Elements.Notes: If each run succeeds with probability p, the expected number of restarts needed is roughly 1/p; for 8-queens, a handful of restarts almost always finds a solution.

Items.Text: Each restart is independent, so the chance of eventually reaching a good optimum rises with the number of trials.
It is trivially parallelisable because restarts do not share information.
The approach is complete with probability approaching 1 given enough restarts.
Cost grows linearly with the number of restarts, so a cap or time budget is usually imposed.

Elements.Title: Comparing the Variants
Elements.BodyText: The variants differ mainly in how much of the neighbourhood they inspect and how much randomness they inject. Choosing among them is a trade-off between cost per step, solution quality, and robustness.
Elements.Notes: In practice, a hybrid such as random-restart first-choice hill climbing performs well on large problems with huge branching factors.

Items.Text: Steepest ascent gives the strongest per-step progress but the highest evaluation cost.
First-choice reduces per-step cost and suits problems with very many successors.
Stochastic hill climbing explores more widely and is less likely to follow a single poor path.
Random restart is the simplest effective remedy for local optima and can wrap any of the other variants.
All variants remain incomplete on their own, since none can escape a local optimum without restarting or accepting downhill moves.

Topics.Title: Local Maxima, Plateaus, and Ridges
Topics.Summary: Examines the characteristic failure modes of greedy local search, including getting trapped on local maxima, wandering on plateaus and shoulders, and zig-zagging along ridges. Reviews mitigation strategies such as sideways moves, restarts, and tabu or memory-based techniques.

Elements.Title: The Local Search Landscape
Elements.BodyText: Local search can be pictured as a journey across a state-space landscape where elevation represents objective value. The shape of this landscape determines whether greedy ascent succeeds or stalls.
Elements.Notes: For a maximization problem, elevation corresponds to the objective function; for minimization, elevation corresponds to cost and the goal becomes finding the lowest valley.

Items.Text: Each point on the landscape is a complete state, and its height is the value assigned by the objective or heuristic function.
A global maximum is the highest peak in the entire landscape and corresponds to the optimal solution.
Hill climbing only perceives the immediate neighbourhood, so it behaves like a climber in dense fog with amnesia.
Because no record of visited states is kept, the algorithm's fate is decided entirely by local gradient information.

Elements.Title: Local Maxima
Elements.BodyText: A local maximum is a peak that is higher than every neighbouring state but lower than the global maximum. Greedy hill climbing halts there because no neighbour offers an improvement.
Elements.Notes: In the 8-queens problem, steepest-ascent hill climbing gets stuck on a local maximum roughly 86% of the time when started from a random state.

Items.Text: The algorithm terminates and reports a suboptimal solution with no indication that a better one exists.
Local maxima are the single most common cause of hill-climbing failure in practice.
The deeper the surrounding 'valleys', the harder it is for small perturbations to escape the peak.
Escaping requires accepting a temporarily worse state, which pure greedy search refuses to do.

Elements.Title: Plateaus and Shoulders
Elements.BodyText: A plateau is a flat region of the landscape where many neighbouring states share the same objective value. The search has no gradient to follow and can wander aimlessly.
Elements.Notes: Distinguishing a shoulder from a flat local maximum cannot be done locally, which is why sideways moves must be bounded.

Items.Text: A flat local maximum is a plateau with no uphill exit, so progress is impossible from there.
A shoulder is a plateau that does have an uphill exit somewhere along its edge, so persistence pays off.
Strict hill climbing stops on any plateau because no neighbour is strictly better.
Random walking across a plateau can consume large amounts of time without improving the objective.

Elements.Title: Ridges and Zig-Zagging
Elements.BodyText: A ridge is a narrow, sloping sequence of local maxima that ascends toward a peak but is difficult to traverse with axis-aligned moves. The result is slow, oscillating progress.
Elements.Notes: Ridges arise when the useful direction of improvement is a diagonal combination of several variables rather than a change to any single variable.

Items.Text: Each individual move off the ridge crest leads downhill, so the search sees no improving step.
The algorithm zig-zags back and forth, making tiny net gains with many wasted evaluations.
Ridges are common in continuous optimization where variables are strongly correlated.
Larger or compound neighbourhood operators can sometimes cut across a ridge in a single move.

Elements.Title: Sideways Moves and Bounded Persistence
Elements.BodyText: Allowing moves to neighbours of equal value lets the search cross shoulders instead of stopping at the first flat spot. A limit on consecutive sideways moves prevents infinite looping.
Elements.Notes: In 8-queens, permitting up to 100 consecutive sideways moves raises the success rate from about 14% to roughly 94%, at the cost of more steps per trial.

Items.Text: Without a bound, the algorithm can loop forever on a flat local maximum.
A typical implementation caps the number of consecutive non-improving moves before declaring failure.
Sideways moves trade additional computation time for a substantially higher success rate.
They help with plateaus but do nothing to escape a true local maximum surrounded by lower states.

Elements.Title: Random Restarts and Stochastic Variants
Elements.BodyText: Restarting the search from fresh random initial states is a simple and powerful remedy for local optima. Injecting randomness into move selection serves a similar purpose.
Elements.Notes: If each trial succeeds with probability p, the expected number of restarts needed is about 1/p, making restarts effective whenever p is not vanishingly small.

Items.Text: Random-restart hill climbing is trivially complete in the limit, since it will eventually generate a goal state.
Stochastic hill climbing chooses among uphill moves with probability proportional to steepness, converging more slowly but often to better optima.
First-choice hill climbing generates successors randomly and takes the first improvement, which suits states with very many neighbours.
Restarts are embarrassingly parallel and easy to combine with any other hill-climbing variant.

Elements.Title: Tabu Search and Memory-Based Escape
Elements.BodyText: Tabu search augments local search with a short-term memory of recently visited states or moves, which are temporarily forbidden. This forces the search out of basins of attraction it would otherwise revisit.
Elements.Notes: Aspiration criteria allow a tabu move to be taken anyway if it would produce a state better than any seen so far.

Items.Text: A tabu list of fixed length stores recent moves or state attributes and blocks their reversal.
Prohibiting backtracking compels the search to accept worsening moves and thereby leave local maxima.
Tabu tenure is a tuning parameter: too short permits cycling, too long over-constrains the search.
Memory-based methods complement randomized approaches such as simulated annealing rather than replacing them.

Topics.Title: Simulated Annealing and Cooling Schedules
Topics.Summary: Presents simulated annealing as a stochastic local search that occasionally accepts worsening moves with a temperature-dependent probability. Details the Metropolis acceptance criterion, the role of the cooling schedule, and conditions under which the method converges to a global optimum.

Elements.Title: Motivation: Escaping Local Optima
Elements.BodyText: Simulated annealing was designed to overcome the central weakness of hill climbing, which halts at the first local maximum, plateau, or ridge it encounters.
Elements.Notes: The name and intuition come from metallurgy: heating a metal and cooling it slowly lets atoms settle into a low-energy crystalline structure, whereas rapid quenching freezes in defects.

Items.Text: Pure hill climbing is efficient but incomplete because it never accepts a worsening move.
A pure random walk is complete in the limit but hopelessly inefficient.
Simulated annealing blends the two: it is mostly greedy but occasionally takes downhill steps.
Early 'hot' exploration lets the search wander out of shallow basins before committing to a region.
Treating the objective as an energy landscape, the goal is to settle into the deepest valley (or highest peak).

Elements.Title: The Simulated Annealing Algorithm
Elements.BodyText: Simulated annealing repeatedly picks one random neighbour of the current state rather than evaluating the full neighbourhood, then decides probabilistically whether to move there.
Elements.Notes: Pseudocode outline: current <- initial state; for t = 1 to infinity: T <- schedule(t); if T = 0 return current; next <- random successor of current; dE <- VALUE(next) - VALUE(current); if dE > 0 then current <- next else current <- next with probability e^(dE/T).

Items.Text: A temperature parameter T is read from a cooling schedule on every iteration.
A single successor is sampled at random, which keeps each iteration cheap.
The change in objective value, ΔE, is computed between the candidate and the current state.
Improving moves (ΔE > 0 for maximisation) are always accepted.
Worsening moves are accepted only with a temperature-dependent probability.
The loop terminates when the temperature reaches zero or a time/iteration budget is exhausted.

Elements.Title: The Metropolis Acceptance Criterion
Elements.BodyText: The probability of accepting a worsening move is e^(-|ΔE|/T), the Metropolis criterion borrowed from statistical physics.
Elements.Notes: Worked example: with T = 10 and ΔE = -1, acceptance probability is e^(-0.1) ≈ 0.90; with T = 0.1 and the same ΔE, it falls to e^(-10) ≈ 0.000045.

Items.Text: Acceptance probability decreases exponentially as the move gets worse (larger |ΔE|).
Acceptance probability also decreases as the temperature T falls.
At high T almost every proposed move is accepted, producing near-random exploration.
At T approaching 0 the algorithm degenerates into stochastic hill climbing.
Small downhill steps are far more likely to be accepted than large ones, so the search rarely abandons a good region entirely.

Elements.Title: The Cooling Schedule
Elements.BodyText: The cooling schedule is the function mapping iteration number to temperature, and it governs the trade-off between exploration and exploitation.
Elements.Notes: Common schedules include geometric cooling T(t) = T0 · α^t with α typically between 0.8 and 0.99, linear cooling, and logarithmic cooling T(t) = c / log(1 + t).

Items.Text: Key parameters are the initial temperature, the decay rule, and the stopping temperature.
Cooling too quickly 'quenches' the search and traps it in a poor local optimum.
Cooling too slowly wastes computation on aimless random wandering.
Geometric (exponential) cooling is the most widely used in practice because it is simple and tunable.
Initial temperature is often calibrated so that roughly 80–90% of proposed moves are accepted at the start.
Reheating or restarts can be added when the search appears to have stagnated.

Elements.Title: Convergence Guarantees
Elements.BodyText: Simulated annealing has a theoretical guarantee of finding the global optimum, but only under conditions that are impractical to satisfy.
Elements.Notes: The logarithmic schedule T(t) = c / log(1 + t) satisfies the theoretical condition but cools so slowly that an exhaustive search is usually faster.

Items.Text: If the temperature is lowered sufficiently slowly, the algorithm converges to a global optimum with probability approaching 1.
The required schedule decreases logarithmically, demanding an impractically large number of iterations.
Practical implementations use faster schedules and therefore sacrifice the guarantee.
In practice simulated annealing is judged empirically as a high-quality anytime algorithm, not a complete one.
Running multiple independent annealing runs and keeping the best result is a common safeguard.

Elements.Title: Practical Use and Comparison
Elements.BodyText: Simulated annealing is widely applied to large combinatorial optimisation problems where the path to the solution is irrelevant and only the final state matters.
Elements.Notes: Classic applications include VLSI layout and circuit placement, factory floor and job-shop scheduling, the travelling salesperson problem, and airline fleet scheduling.

Items.Text: It requires only a state representation, a neighbour-generating move, and an objective function.
Memory use is constant, as only the current state (and optionally the best-seen state) is stored.
It generally outperforms plain hill climbing on rugged landscapes with many local optima.
Performance is sensitive to tuning of the schedule and the neighbourhood definition.
Related stochastic alternatives include random-restart hill climbing, local beam search, and genetic algorithms.
Always track the best state encountered, since the final state is not guaranteed to be the best visited.

Topics.Title: Applying Local Search to Large-Scale Problems
Topics.Summary: Applies hill climbing and simulated annealing to practical problems such as n-queens, scheduling, VLSI layout, and route optimization. Discusses algorithm selection, parameter tuning, and evaluation of solution quality against computational cost.

Elements.Title: When Local Search Is the Right Tool
Elements.BodyText: Local search suits problems where only the final configuration matters and the path taken to reach it is irrelevant. Large-scale combinatorial problems often make systematic search infeasible, leaving optimization over complete states as the practical option.
Elements.Notes: Classic indicators: enormous or continuous state spaces, no meaningful notion of a 'solution path', and an easily computable objective function.

Items.Text: Choose local search when the goal is a configuration, not a sequence of actions.
Memory use stays constant because only the current state (and perhaps the best seen) is retained.
Problems with cheap incremental evaluation of neighbours benefit most.
If an optimal, provably complete answer is required, systematic search or exact methods may still be preferable.

Elements.Title: N-Queens as a Benchmark Problem
Elements.BodyText: The n-queens problem is the standard demonstration of local search on a complete-state formulation. Each state places one queen per column, and the objective is to minimise the number of attacking pairs.
Elements.Notes: Hill climbing solves large n-queens instances in a handful of steps on average, far faster than backtracking search over partial assignments.

Items.Text: The successor function moves a single queen within its column, giving a manageable neighbourhood size.
The heuristic h counts pairs of queens attacking each other; a solution has h = 0.
Steepest-ascent hill climbing gets stuck on roughly 86% of random instances but succeeds quickly when it does.
Allowing sideways moves on plateaux or restarting from random states raises the success rate dramatically.

Elements.Title: Scheduling, Layout, and Routing Applications
Elements.BodyText: Local search is widely deployed on industrial optimization problems where state spaces are astronomically large. Scheduling, VLSI layout, and vehicle routing are canonical examples.
Elements.Notes: In these domains an approximate solution delivered quickly is usually worth more than an optimal solution delivered too late.

Items.Text: Job-shop and airline scheduling use moves that swap tasks or shift start times to reduce makespan or cost.
VLSI cell layout and channel routing minimise wire length and area through local repositioning of components.
Vehicle routing and travelling-salesperson variants use 2-opt or or-opt moves that reverse or relocate route segments.
Telecommunications network configuration and automatic programming are further established application areas.

Elements.Title: Choosing Between Hill Climbing and Simulated Annealing
Elements.BodyText: Algorithm selection depends on the ruggedness of the objective landscape and the computational budget available. Hill climbing is fast but brittle; simulated annealing trades time for robustness.
Elements.Notes: A practical strategy is to start with random-restart hill climbing as a baseline and escalate to annealing only if the landscape proves rugged.

Items.Text: Use plain or steepest-ascent hill climbing on smooth landscapes with few local optima.
Use random-restart hill climbing when the search is cheap and the probability of success per run is reasonable.
Use simulated annealing when the landscape is rugged and escaping deep local optima matters more than speed.
Use first-choice hill climbing when the branching factor makes enumerating all neighbours too expensive.

Elements.Title: Tuning the Cooling Schedule and Parameters
Elements.BodyText: Simulated annealing's performance is dominated by its cooling schedule and move-generation design. Poor parameter choices can make it behave like random walk or like plain hill climbing.
Elements.Notes: Common schedules include geometric cooling (T ← αT with α typically between 0.8 and 0.99) and logarithmic cooling, which is theoretically optimal but impractically slow.

Items.Text: Set the initial temperature so that most uphill (worsening) moves are accepted early on.
Cool slowly enough that the search equilibrates at each temperature, but fast enough to fit the time budget.
Define a sensible neighbourhood: moves should be small enough to be informative and large enough to traverse the space.
Specify a stopping criterion such as a final temperature, an iteration cap, or a run with no accepted moves.

Elements.Title: Evaluating Solution Quality Against Computational Cost
Elements.BodyText: Local search offers no guarantee of optimality, so evaluation must balance achieved objective value against the time and iterations consumed. Empirical benchmarking replaces theoretical completeness guarantees.
Elements.Notes: Report results over many random seeds, since a single run of a stochastic algorithm says little about expected performance.

Items.Text: Measure mean and best objective value across repeated runs, not a single lucky execution.
Track success rate (fraction of runs reaching an acceptable threshold) and average number of evaluations per run.
Plot anytime curves showing best-so-far quality versus elapsed time to compare algorithms fairly.
Compare against a known optimum, a lower bound, or a baseline heuristic to judge the quality gap.
Accept diminishing returns: extra computation often yields only marginal improvement near the end of a run.
